questions.explanation: Global object g is constructed during static initialization before main() runs, so 'boot' is printed first, then 'main'.

questions.question: A `Buffer` class owning a `new[]`'d pointer crashes on double-delete after `Buffer b = a;` — a reviewer insists that because it needs a destructor it must also declare the copy constructor and copy assignment — which rule is this?
questions.explanation: If a class needs any of destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment, it almost certainly needs all three: the rule of three.

questions.question: Extending the rule of three so a resource-owning class supports `std::move(a)` transfers instead of deep copies adds a move constructor and move assignment — under which C++11 guideline are all five declared?
questions.explanation: C++11 move semantics extend the rule of three: destructor, copy ctor, copy assign, move ctor, move assign — the rule of five.
data is populated only on the first get() call and cached afterward: lazy initialization.
lock_guard's destructor runs during stack unwinding, tying the mutex's release to object lifetime: RAII.

questions.question: `Query.select("*").from("users").where("age > 18").limit(10)` assembles a complex object through chained calls before producing the final Query — which creational pattern is this?
questions.explanation: A fluent interface configures the product step by step, then builds it: the Builder pattern.

questions.question: In C++, `char buf[sizeof(S)];` followed by `S* p = new (buf) S();` constructs an S inside caller-supplied storage — which form of new is this?
questions.explanation: new (buf) S() is placement new: it runs the constructor at the given address without allocating memory.
C's only constructor requires x; with no default constructor available, calling C() raises TypeError.
S() forwards its initialization to S(int): a delegating constructor, introduced in C++11.

questions.question: A game engine returns Bullet objects to a freelist on `release()` and reissues them from `acquire()` instead of allocating per shot — which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Reusing a bounded set of pre-constructed objects rather than repeatedly creating and destroying them is object pooling.

questions.question: In Java, class A has A() calling this(5) and A(int x) printing x — what does new A() print?
questions.explanation: Constructor chaining with this(5) invokes A(int x) which prints 5.
Members initialize in declaration order, not initializer-list order: a is initialized first from the still-uninitialized b, leaving a indeterminate while b becomes 1.
The copy constructor is marked = delete; copy-initializing b attempts to call it, so compilation fails.
__init__ runs only when __new__ returns an instance of the class; returning 42 skips __init__, so A() yields 42 and 'init' never prints.

questions.question: `struct Config { std::string name; std::vector<int> opts; };` owns no raw resources, so the team declares no destructor, copy, or move members and lets the compiler generate them — which C++ guideline supports this?
questions.explanation: When every member manages its own resources, compiler-generated special members are already correct — declare none: the rule of zero.

questions.question: In Java, what is printed by `class A { { System.out.println("I"); } A() { System.out.println("C"); } } class B extends A { { System.out.println("i"); } B() { System.out.println("c"); } }` on `new B()`?
questions.explanation: Order: parent instance initializer, parent constructor, child instance initializer, child constructor.

questions.question: A Java constructor contains `super(); this(5);` — what is the result?
questions.explanation: this() must be the first statement; combining it with super() is illegal.

questions.question: The default C++ copy constructor copies a pointer member — what kind of copy results when you duplicate such an object?
questions.explanation: Only the pointer value is copied; both objects share the same pointee.

questions.question: In Python, what happens if `__init__` returns a non-None value such as `return self`?
questions.explanation: Python raises TypeError: __init__() should return None.

questions.question: You define `class C { C(int x) {} }` in Java and call `new C()` — what happens?
questions.explanation: Once any constructor is declared, no default constructor is generated, so new C() fails to compile.
